methods.label: Clarify the hypothesis and give a counterexample
methods.explanation:
Assume the intended meaning is that perpendicularity to one specified line in the plane is all that is known.

One line is not enough; it may only be perpendicular to one particular direction.

For a counterexample, take perpendicular lines \(l\) and \(m\) lying in the same plane \(\alpha\). Although \(l\perp m\), the line \(l\) is not perpendicular to \(\alpha\): that would require perpendicularity to every direction in \(\alpha\), including its own direction.

If “only one line” instead means exactly one line in \(\alpha\), the hypothesis is impossible. Perpendicularity of spatial lines is determined by their directions, so every line in \(\alpha\) parallel to \(m\) is also perpendicular to \(l\). There are infinitely many such lines. Thus the literal wording describes no possible configuration; under the intended reading, the answer is C. No.
methods.levelReason: The argument uses elementary perpendicularity, parallel lines, plane containment, and the direction-based definition of line-plane perpendicularity, all within Required mathematics II or earlier material.
